units.title: Thinking Like a Historian
units.blurb: How historians know what they know: primary and secondary sources, reading a source for its situation, audience, purpose and point of view, dates and periods, and causes and effects.

units.title: Native America and Contact (1491 to 1607)
units.blurb: The peoples of the Americas before 1492, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange and the Spanish empire. AP Period 1.

units.title: Colonial America (1607 to 1754)
units.blurb: Jamestown and the Chesapeake, New England, the Middle and Southern colonies, slavery, conflict with Native nations, the empire's trade rules, religion and the Enlightenment, and colonial self-government. AP Period 2.

units.title: The American Revolution (1754 to 1783)
units.blurb: The French and Indian War, new British taxes and colonial protest, the outbreak of war, the Declaration of Independence, the war itself, the peace and what the Revolution changed. AP Period 3.

units.title: From Confederation to Constitution (1781 to 1800)
units.blurb: The Articles of Confederation, the Northwest Ordinance, Shays' Rebellion, the Constitutional Convention, the ratification fight, the Bill of Rights, and the first presidents and parties. AP Period 3.

units.title: The Early Republic (1800 to 1848)
units.blurb: Jefferson and the Louisiana Purchase, the Marshall Court, the War of 1812, the Monroe years, the market revolution, Jacksonian democracy, Indian removal, religious revival and reform. AP Period 4.

units.title: Expansion and the Sectional Crisis (1844 to 1861)
units.blurb: Manifest Destiny, Texas, Oregon and the war with Mexico, gold and immigration, the compromises over slavery in the territories, Dred Scott, Lincoln and secession. AP Period 5.

units.title: The Civil War and Reconstruction (1861 to 1877)
units.blurb: The two sides, the war's turning points, emancipation, the home fronts, Lincoln's words, Reconstruction and the amendments, and how Reconstruction ended. AP Period 5.

topics.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
topics.short: A primary source was made at the time by someone who saw or took part (a letter, a law, a photo); a secondary source was made later by someone studying it (a textbook, a history book).
topics.trouble: Students call any old source primary, or think primary sources are always true. A 1900 history of the Revolution is old but secondary; a primary source shows one person's view and must be checked like any other.

topics.title: Reading a Source: HIPP
topics.short: Ask four questions of any source: its Historical situation, Intended audience, Purpose and Point of view; each one shapes what the source says and leaves out.
topics.trouble: Students summarize what a source says but never ask why it was written or for whom. A speech to supporters and a private letter by the same person can say different things for good reasons.

topics.title: Dates, Centuries and Periods
topics.short: The 1700s are the 18th century; historians group years into periods (such as 1754 to 1800) around big turning points, and a timeline shows what came before what.
topics.trouble: Students think the 1800s are the 18th century. The 18th century is the 1700s (1701 to 1800): add one to the hundreds digit.

topics.title: Causes, Effects and Change Over Time
topics.short: Big events usually have several causes, long-term and short-term, and several effects; historians also ask what changed and what stayed the same.
topics.trouble: Students name one cause for an event, or treat whatever came just before an event as its cause. Look for long-term conditions as well as the spark, and check that a cause actually led to the effect.

topics.title: The First Peoples of the Americas
topics.short: People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago, by land across Beringia, along the Pacific coast, or both; the exact dates and routes are still studied and debated.
topics.trouble: Students treat a single date or route as settled. Archaeologists agree people came from northeast Asia over thousands of years; they debate when and by which routes as new sites are dated.

topics.title: Native Cultures Across North America
topics.short: By 1491 Native societies across North America had adapted to very different lands: maize farming and irrigation in the Southwest, hunting and farming on the Plains, fishing in the Northwest, mixed farming and villages in the East.
topics.trouble: Students picture Plains peoples on horseback before Columbus. Horses came with the Spanish; Plains horse cultures grew in the 1600s and 1700s.

topics.title: Cities, Confederacies and Pueblos
topics.short: Some Native societies built large towns and alliances: Cahokia, a Mississippian city near present-day St. Louis; the Ancestral Puebloans of the Four Corners; the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy of the Northeast.
topics.trouble: Students assume complex towns and governments came only from Europe. Cahokia may have had 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100; the Haudenosaunee Confederacy united several nations under a shared council.

topics.title: Why Europeans Explored
topics.short: Portugal and Spain sought sea routes to Asian trade, new wealth, the spread of Christianity and national glory; Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided claims between Spain and Portugal.
topics.trouble: Students think Europeans set out to find the Americas. Columbus was trying to reach Asia by sailing west and believed to the end that he had reached Asian islands.

topics.title: The Columbian Exchange
topics.short: After 1492 plants, animals, people and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways: horses, wheat and cattle to the Americas; maize, potatoes and tomatoes to Europe, Africa and Asia; and diseases such as smallpox that killed a large share of Native peoples.
topics.trouble: Students think the exchange went one way, or that Native deaths came mostly from war. Epidemic diseases to which Native peoples had no immunity caused most of the population collapse.

topics.title: The Spanish Empire in the Americas
topics.short: Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec (1521) and Inca empires; Spain ruled through the encomienda system and missions, founded St. Augustine (1565), and debated how Native peoples should be treated.
topics.trouble: Students think the Spanish conquest happened by a handful of soldiers alone. Native allies, epidemics and divisions among Native states were decisive; Bartolomé de las Casas and others protested the abuses.

topics.title: Jamestown and the Chesapeake
topics.short: Jamestown (1607) survived hard early years and grew rich on tobacco; Virginia set up the House of Burgesses in 1619, the same year the first recorded Africans arrived in the colony.
topics.trouble: Students think Jamestown thrived from the start. Most early settlers died; the "starving time" of 1609 to 1610 nearly ended it, and tobacco and the headright system made it last.

topics.title: Pilgrims and Puritans in New England
topics.short: The Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact (1620) and founded Plymouth; Puritans founded Massachusetts Bay (1630); dissenters such as Roger Williams (Rhode Island, 1636) and Anne Hutchinson were banished.
topics.trouble: Students think the Puritans came to found a land of religious freedom for all. They sought freedom to practice their own faith and expected others in their colony to conform.

topics.title: The Middle Colonies
topics.short: New York (Dutch New Netherland until 1664), New Jersey, Pennsylvania (founded by William Penn, a Quaker, in 1681) and Delaware were the most diverse colonies, with wheat farms, ports and wide religious toleration.
topics.trouble: Students think all colonies were English from the start and all alike. New York began as Dutch; the Middle colonies mixed Dutch, English, German, Scots-Irish and other settlers and many faiths.

topics.title: The Southern Colonies
topics.short: Maryland (1634) was a refuge for English Catholics; the Carolinas grew rice and indigo on plantations worked by enslaved Africans; Georgia (1732) was the last of the thirteen.
topics.trouble: Students think every Southern colonist owned a plantation. Most white Southerners were small farmers; large plantations held most of the enslaved people.

topics.title: Comparing the Colonial Regions
topics.short: Compare New England (towns, trade, fishing, small farms), the Middle colonies (wheat, ports, diversity) and the South (cash crops, plantations, slavery) and explain why geography and settlers made them differ.
topics.trouble: Students sort colonies by memory of one fact. Tie each region's economy to its land and climate: rocky soil and short summers in New England, fertile valleys in the Middle colonies, long growing seasons in the South.

topics.title: Slavery in the Colonies
topics.short: Enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage; colonial slave codes made slavery lifelong and inherited through the mother; enslaved people resisted, as in the Stono Rebellion of 1739.
topics.trouble: Students think slavery existed only in the Southern colonies, or that it was fixed by law from 1619. Slavery was legal in all thirteen colonies, and Virginia's laws making it hereditary came in the 1660s.

topics.title: Colonists and Native Nations in Conflict
topics.short: As colonies spread, wars broke out: the Pequot War (1636 to 1638), King Philip's (Metacom's) War (1675 to 1676), Bacon's Rebellion against Virginia's governor (1676) and the Pueblo Revolt against Spain (1680).
topics.trouble: Students treat Native nations as only victims or only enemies. Nations made alliances, traded, fought and negotiated to protect their lands; the Pueblo Revolt drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years.

topics.title: Mercantilism and the Navigation Acts
topics.short: Under mercantilism, colonies existed to enrich the mother country; the Navigation Acts (from 1651) made colonists ship key goods only on English ships to English ports, though Britain enforced them loosely for decades ("salutary neglect").
topics.trouble: Students confuse mercantilism with free trade. Mercantilism aimed at a favorable balance of trade for the mother country through controls on colonial trade.

topics.title: The Great Awakening and the Enlightenment
topics.short: The First Great Awakening (1730s and 1740s, Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield) brought revival preaching and new churches; Enlightenment ideas of reason and natural rights (John Locke) spread through books, Benjamin Franklin and colonial colleges.
topics.trouble: Students treat the two movements as the same. The Awakening was religious revival based on personal faith; the Enlightenment stressed reason and science. Both encouraged colonists to question authority.

topics.title: Colonial Self-Government
topics.short: Colonists grew used to governing themselves through elected assemblies such as the House of Burgesses, New England town meetings and colonial legislatures that controlled taxes; the Zenger trial (1735) defended printing criticism of officials.
topics.trouble: Students think the colonists had no say in government before 1776. They had elected assemblies for over a century; their protest was against Parliament taxing them without those assemblies' consent.

topics.title: The French and Indian War
topics.short: Britain and France fought for North America from 1754 to 1763 (part of the Seven Years' War); Britain won Canada and the land east of the Mississippi, but its war debt and the Proclamation of 1763 set the stage for conflict with the colonists.
topics.trouble: Students think the war was between the French and the Native peoples. The name comes from the British colonists' enemies, the French and their Native allies; many Native nations fought on both sides.

topics.title: New Taxes and Colonial Protest
topics.short: To pay the war debt, Parliament passed the Sugar Act (1764), Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend Acts (1767); colonists answered with the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts and the cry "no taxation without representation."
topics.trouble: Students think the colonists objected mostly to how high the taxes were. Many British taxes were low; the colonists objected that Parliament, where they had no members, had no right to tax them at all.

topics.title: The Road to Revolution
topics.short: Tension grew from the Boston Massacre (1770) to the Tea Act and Boston Tea Party (1773), the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts (1774) and the First Continental Congress (1774).
topics.trouble: Students put the events out of order or think the Tea Party protested a new tax increase. The Tea Act actually lowered the price of tea; colonists objected that it kept the tax and favored the East India Company.

topics.title: Lexington, Concord and Common Sense
topics.short: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775; the Second Continental Congress made George Washington commander; Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776) argued for full independence.
topics.trouble: Students think the war began after the Declaration of Independence. The fighting began more than a year earlier; many colonists at first hoped only to restore their rights within the empire.

topics.title: The Declaration of Independence
topics.short: Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and adopted the Declaration on July 4; written mainly by Thomas Jefferson, it states a theory of government by consent, lists grievances against the King and declares the colonies free.
topics.trouble: Students think the Declaration set up the new government. It explains why the colonies separated; the Articles of Confederation and later the Constitution set up the government.

topics.title: Patriots, Loyalists and Neutrals
topics.short: Colonists divided: Patriots backed independence, Loyalists stayed loyal to Britain, many stayed neutral; Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offered freedom to enslaved people who joined the British, and most Native nations sided with Britain.
topics.trouble: Students think nearly all colonists supported independence. Historians estimate roughly a fifth were Loyalists, and many others tried to stay out of the war.

topics.title: Winning the War
topics.short: Key moments: Washington's victory at Trenton (1776), the American win at Saratoga (1777) that brought the French alliance (1778), the hard winter at Valley Forge (1777 to 1778) and the British surrender at Yorktown (1781).
topics.trouble: Students think the Americans won mainly by defeating the British in big battles. They won by keeping their army alive, winning key fights, and gaining French money, troops and ships.

topics.title: The Treaty of Paris, 1783
topics.short: In the Treaty of Paris (1783) Britain recognized American independence, with borders at the Mississippi River in the west, Canada in the north and Spanish Florida in the south.
topics.trouble: Students think the war ended with Yorktown in 1781. Fighting dwindled after Yorktown, but the treaty that ended the war came two years later.

topics.title: What the Revolution Changed
topics.short: The Revolution brought new state constitutions with bills of rights, the gradual abolition of slavery in Northern states (beginning with Pennsylvania in 1780), Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom (1786) and new ideas about women as "republican mothers."
topics.trouble: Students think the Revolution changed everything or changed nothing for those left out. Change was real but uneven: Northern states ended slavery gradually, while Southern states kept it, and voting was still mostly limited to men with property.

topics.title: The Articles of Confederation
topics.short: The Articles (in force 1781) set up a weak national government: one vote per state in Congress, no executive or national courts, no power to tax, nine states to pass key laws and all thirteen to amend.
topics.trouble: Students think the Articles accomplished nothing. They won the war, made peace and organized western lands; their weakness was a Congress that could not tax or enforce its laws.

topics.title: The Land Ordinance and the Northwest Ordinance
topics.short: The Land Ordinance of 1785 surveyed western land into square townships; the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 set out how territories become states equal to the old ones and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.
topics.trouble: Students think new states joined as colonies of the original thirteen. The Ordinance promised that new states would join "on an equal footing" with the original states.

topics.title: Shays' Rebellion
topics.short: In 1786 and 1787 indebted Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays closed courts to stop foreclosures; the weak national government could do little, which convinced many leaders to strengthen it.
topics.trouble: Students think Shays' Rebellion was a battle with Britain. It was an uprising of Americans against their own state over debts and taxes.

topics.title: The Constitutional Convention
topics.short: In 1787 delegates in Philadelphia replaced the Articles; the Great (Connecticut) Compromise blended the Virginia Plan (seats by population) and the New Jersey Plan (equal seats), and other compromises dealt with slavery and the presidency.
topics.trouble: Students think the Three-Fifths Compromise said enslaved people were three-fifths of a person in law. It was a rule for counting population for House seats and direct taxes: three of every five enslaved people were counted.

topics.title: Federalists, Anti-Federalists and Ratification
topics.short: Federalists (Madison, Hamilton, Jay, writing as "Publius" in The Federalist) defended the Constitution; Anti-Federalists (such as "Brutus" and the "Federal Farmer") feared a distant, too-strong government without a bill of rights; New Hampshire's ratification in June 1788 made nine states.
topics.trouble: Students think the Anti-Federalists opposed having any national government, or lost every point. Most wanted a stronger union with firmer limits; their push for a bill of rights succeeded in 1791.

topics.title: The Bill of Rights
topics.short: James Madison drafted amendments in the First Congress (1789); ten were ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights, protecting freedoms such as speech, religion, the press and fair trials from the national government.
topics.trouble: Students think the Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution of 1787, or that it limited the states from the start. It was added in 1791, and at first it limited only the national government.

topics.title: Washington Sets the Pattern
topics.short: Washington (1789 to 1797) formed the first Cabinet, backed Alexander Hamilton's plan (paying state war debts, a national bank, tariffs), put down the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), kept the country neutral in Europe's wars, and stepped down after two terms.
topics.trouble: Students think the two-term limit was in the Constitution from the start. Washington chose to step down; the Twenty-second Amendment made the limit law in 1951.

topics.title: The First Political Parties
topics.short: Disputes over Hamilton's plans and the French Revolution split leaders into Federalists (Hamilton, Adams: a strong national government, commerce, ties to Britain) and Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison: strict reading of the Constitution, farmers, sympathy for France).
topics.trouble: Students think the founders planned on parties or that today's parties go straight back to them. Washington warned against parties; today's Democratic Party traces to Jefferson's and Jackson's coalitions, and today's Republican Party began in 1854.

topics.title: John Adams and the Election of 1800
topics.short: Under John Adams came the XYZ Affair, an undeclared naval war with France, and the Alien and Sedition Acts (1798), which Jefferson and Madison opposed in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions; in 1800 power passed peacefully from one party to the other.
topics.trouble: Students miss why 1800 mattered. It was the first time power passed from one party to another by an election, peacefully; it also exposed the electoral tie that led to the Twelfth Amendment (1804).

topics.title: Jefferson and the Louisiana Purchase
topics.short: In 1803 Jefferson bought Louisiana from France for about $15 million, roughly doubling the country's size, and sent Lewis and Clark (1804 to 1806) to explore it, though he doubted the Constitution clearly allowed the purchase.
topics.trouble: Students think the purchase was only the present state of Louisiana. It covered the land from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains, all or part of fifteen later states.

topics.title: The Marshall Court
topics.short: Chief Justice John Marshall (1801 to 1835) strengthened the courts and the national government: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review, McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) upheld the national bank, Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) read the commerce power broadly.
topics.trouble: Students think the Constitution says in so many words that courts may strike down laws. Judicial review is not spelled out; Marshall reasoned it from the Constitution being supreme law and judges' duty to say what the law is.

topics.title: The War of 1812
topics.short: Over British impressment of sailors, trade limits and support for Native resistance in the West, the U.S. went to war with Britain (1812 to 1815); the British burned Washington, Fort McHenry held, and the Treaty of Ghent restored prewar borders.
topics.trouble: Students think the Battle of New Orleans won the war. It came in January 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent had been signed (December 1814) but before news of it arrived.

topics.title: Good Feelings, Missouri and the Monroe Doctrine
topics.short: Under Monroe one party dominated; Henry Clay's "American System" proposed a bank, tariffs and roads and canals; the Missouri Compromise (1820) balanced slave and free states and drew the 36°30' line; the Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against new colonies in the Americas.
topics.trouble: Students think the Missouri Compromise settled slavery in the West for good. It postponed the conflict; it was repealed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854.

topics.title: The Market Revolution
topics.short: Canals (the Erie Canal, 1825), steamboats and railroads tied regions into a national market; textile mills (Lowell) grew in the North, while the cotton gin (1793) and world demand spread cotton and slavery across the Deep South.
topics.trouble: Students think the cotton gin reduced slavery by saving labor. It made short-staple cotton profitable, so cotton planting and the number of enslaved people both grew rapidly.

topics.title: Jacksonian Democracy
topics.short: Most states dropped property rules for white men voting; Andrew Jackson (1829 to 1837) used the spoils system, vetoed the Second Bank's recharter (1832) and faced down South Carolina in the Nullification Crisis (1832 to 1833); Democrats and Whigs formed the second party system.
topics.trouble: Students think "democracy" expanded to everyone in this era. Voting widened for white men, while free Black men lost the vote in several states and women could not vote.

topics.title: Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears
topics.short: The Indian Removal Act (1830) led to the forced removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole nations west of the Mississippi; despite Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Cherokee were forced out in 1838 and 1839 on the Trail of Tears, and thousands died.
topics.trouble: Students think the Supreme Court approved removal. In Worcester v. Georgia the Court ruled for the Cherokee that Georgia law did not apply in their nation; the ruling was not enforced.

topics.title: Revival and Reform
topics.short: The Second Great Awakening (about 1800 to the 1840s) inspired reform movements: temperance, public schools (Horace Mann), better care for the mentally ill (Dorothea Dix), prison reform and utopian communities.
topics.trouble: Students separate religion from the reform movements. Many reformers were driven by the revival's belief that people could improve themselves and society.

topics.title: The Abolition Movement
topics.short: Abolitionists such as William Lloyd Garrison (The Liberator, 1831), Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth and the Grimké sisters demanded an end to slavery; Nat Turner's revolt (1831) and the Underground Railroad showed enslaved people's resistance.
topics.trouble: Students think most Northerners were abolitionists. Abolitionists were a small, often unpopular minority before the 1850s; many more Northerners opposed only the spread of slavery.

topics.title: Seneca Falls and Women's Rights
topics.short: At Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848 Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott and others issued the Declaration of Sentiments, modeled on the Declaration of Independence, which demanded rights for women including the vote.
topics.trouble: Students think women won the vote soon after Seneca Falls. The national amendment came 72 years later, in 1920.

topics.title: Manifest Destiny
topics.short: The idea that the United States was destined to spread across the continent (named in 1845) drove the annexation of Texas (independent from Mexico since 1836) in 1845 and the Oregon treaty with Britain (1846) at the 49th parallel.
topics.trouble: Students treat Manifest Destiny as a law or a treaty. It was a belief and a slogan; the land came by treaty, purchase, annexation and war.

topics.title: The Mexican-American War
topics.short: After a border dispute, the U.S. fought Mexico (1846 to 1848); in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo Mexico ceded California and the Southwest; the Wilmot Proviso to ban slavery in that land passed the House but failed in the Senate.
topics.trouble: Students think the war was widely popular. Many Whigs, abolitionists and others (Abraham Lincoln and Henry David Thoreau among them) opposed it.

topics.title: How the Country Grew
topics.short: Match each addition to its year and how it came: the 1783 treaty lands, Louisiana (1803), Florida (1819), Texas (1845), Oregon (1846), the Mexican Cession (1848), the Gadsden Purchase (1853), and later Alaska (1867) and Hawaii (1898).
topics.trouble: Students think the country grew mostly by war. Most land came by treaty or purchase; the Mexican Cession followed a war, and the land of Native nations was taken by many treaties and removals.

topics.title: Gold, Immigrants and Nativism
topics.short: The California Gold Rush (1849) drew people from around the world; Irish (after the 1845 famine) and German immigrants poured into the North; nativists formed the anti-immigrant American ("Know-Nothing") Party.
topics.trouble: Students think immigration began with Ellis Island. The 1840s and 1850s saw one of the largest waves, measured against the population, in the country's history.

topics.title: The Compromise of 1850
topics.short: California joined as a free state; New Mexico and Utah would decide slavery by popular sovereignty; the slave trade (not slavery) ended in the District of Columbia; a stronger Fugitive Slave Act angered the North, and Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) moved many readers.
topics.trouble: Students think the Compromise ended slavery in Washington, D.C. It ended the buying and selling of enslaved people there; slavery in the District ended in 1862.

topics.title: Kansas-Nebraska and Bleeding Kansas
topics.short: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) let settlers vote on slavery, repealing the Missouri line; violence in "Bleeding Kansas" followed, and opponents of slavery's spread founded the Republican Party (1854).
topics.trouble: Students think the Republican Party was founded to abolish slavery everywhere. Its founding goal was to stop slavery from spreading into the territories.

topics.title: The Dred Scott Decision
topics.short: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) the Supreme Court held 7 to 2 that Black Americans were not citizens who could sue in federal court and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories; the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) overturned the citizenship ruling.
topics.trouble: Students think the decision settled the dispute. It inflamed it: it struck at the core of the Republican platform and was widely denounced in the North.

topics.title: Lincoln, John Brown and the Election of 1860
topics.short: Lincoln and Stephen Douglas debated slavery in 1858; John Brown raided Harpers Ferry in 1859; in 1860 Lincoln won the presidency in a four-way race with no electoral votes from the Deep South.
topics.trouble: Students think Lincoln ran promising to abolish slavery in the states. He pledged not to interfere with slavery where it existed but to stop its spread.

topics.title: Secession and Fort Sumter
topics.short: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, followed by six more Deep South states that formed the Confederacy in February 1861; after Confederates fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, four more states seceded, while slave-holding border states stayed in the Union.
topics.trouble: Students think all slave states seceded at once. Seven left before Lincoln took office, four after Fort Sumter, and four (Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri) stayed in the Union.

topics.title: The Union and the Confederacy
topics.short: The Union had far more people, factories and railroads; the Confederacy fought on its own ground with skilled generals; the Union's Anaconda Plan aimed to blockade the coast and seize the Mississippi.
topics.trouble: Students think the Union's advantages made the outcome certain. The Confederacy only had to survive until the North gave up; Union victory took four years and depended on battlefield results and Northern will.

topics.title: Turning Points of the War
topics.short: Key events: Bull Run (1861), Antietam (1862), Gettysburg and the fall of Vicksburg (July 1863), Sherman's capture of Atlanta and March to the Sea (1864), and Lee's surrender at Appomattox (April 1865).
topics.trouble: Students put Gettysburg first or think it ended the war. Gettysburg (July 1863) was a turning point, but the war went on almost two more years.

topics.title: Emancipation
topics.short: The Emancipation Proclamation (January 1, 1863) declared enslaved people free in areas in rebellion and allowed Black men to join the Union army, where about 180,000 served; the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the country.
topics.trouble: Students think the Proclamation freed all enslaved people at once. It applied only to areas in rebellion, not to the loyal border states; freedom came as Union armies advanced and was made permanent by the Thirteenth Amendment.

topics.title: The Home Fronts
topics.short: Both sides drafted soldiers (the New York draft riots, 1863); Lincoln suspended habeas corpus in some areas; Congress passed the Homestead Act, Morrill Land-Grant Act and Pacific Railway Act (1862); women served as nurses and ran farms and businesses.
topics.trouble: Students think only soldiers were affected. The war changed government (an income tax, paper money, conscription) and daily life in both sections.

topics.title: The Gettysburg Address
topics.short: In November 1863 Lincoln dedicated the cemetery at Gettysburg in about 270 words, describing the war as a test of whether a nation "conceived in Liberty" could endure and calling for "a new birth of freedom."
topics.trouble: Students think the speech was long or that it was written on the back of an envelope on the train. It took about two minutes; that envelope story is a legend, and five copies in Lincoln's hand survive.

topics.title: Lincoln's Death and Johnson's Plan
topics.short: Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865; Andrew Johnson's lenient plan let Southern states rejoin quickly, and many passed Black Codes limiting freedpeople's rights.
topics.trouble: Students think Reconstruction began with harsh rule over the South. The first phase under Johnson was lenient to former Confederates; Congress took control in 1867.

topics.title: Reconstruction Under Congress
topics.short: Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau, passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over Johnson's veto, imposed the Reconstruction Acts (1867) and impeached Johnson (1868), who was acquitted by one vote; Black men voted and held office, including Senator Hiram Revels.
topics.trouble: Students think Black officeholders controlled Southern governments. Hundreds served in state legislatures and Congress, but white Republicans held most offices.

topics.title: The Reconstruction Amendments
topics.short: The Thirteenth (1865) ended slavery; the Fourteenth (1868) made all persons born here citizens and promised due process and equal protection; the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote because of race.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the three amendments or think the Fifteenth gave women the vote. It protected voting against racial discrimination only; women won the vote with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

topics.title: The End of Reconstruction
topics.short: Violence by the Ku Klux Klan and others, Northern fatigue and the economic panic of 1873 wore Reconstruction down; the Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed 1876 election and federal troops left the last Southern capitals; sharecropping and segregation laws followed.
topics.trouble: Students think the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments protected Black Southerners from 1870 on. After 1877 they were widely ignored in practice for decades, until the civil rights movement.
